passages.section: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
passages.location: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
passages.text: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)—either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model ( eVLM ). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21 % 0.21\% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5 % 16.5\% – 35.1 % 35.1\% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit , we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15 % 98.15\% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9 % 85.9\% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC–D.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: The premise of vision-language-action (VLA) policies is to transfer the visual perception, semantic grounding, and generalization of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to physical manipulation. Beneath specific design choices lies a foundational question: how can we enable a pretrained VLM to natively output precise continuous actions while preserving its visual-language generalization, its model architecture, and its native training paradigm? Existing VLAs largely compromise on at least one of these requirements by treating action as an external attachment to a VLM—dividing manipulation and cognition across separate representations, modules, or training objectives, where the VLM handles scene and instruction understanding while another mechanism handles action representation, trajectory generation, or coordinate supervision. Our thesis is that manipulation and cognition should not be decoupled across a bolted-on VLA pipeline; they should be embodied in a single Embodied Vision-Language Model ( eVLM ). Concretely, in an eVLM, actions are represented directly in the backbone’s continuous hidden space, generated across time by the same parameters and native generative operator that process vision and language, and supervised in physical coordinates end-to-end without degrading the shared VLM.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: Three principles motivate this shift from decoupled VLAs to a unified eVLM. First, cognition should participate in manipulation at every layer. Grasping, placement, and obstacle avoidance rely on the same spatial and physical cues as scene understanding; when trajectory generation happens outside the VLM, cognition is reduced to a one-time conditioning handoff and cannot interact with evolving action states across depth. Second, manipulation should shape cognition in return. Robot trajectories are the primary source of physical and spatial grounding for a VLM; only when continuous action gradients directly update the vision-language parameters can manipulation experience consolidate into the backbone’s spatial cognition rather than remaining confined to an external head. Third, preserving the backbone’s architecture, training paradigm, and representation stability enables end-to-end scaling. When cognitive and motor modules rely on incompatible paradigms or objectives, their gradients compete and degrade pretrained representations, often forcing practitioners to insulate or freeze the backbone ( Driess et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2025 ) and permanently fixing the separation between perception and control.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: From this perspective, conventional VLAs fail to form a unified eVLM in two primary ways (Table 1 ). The first is representational decoupling . Methods such as RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) quantize each action dimension into discrete bins and reuse the language vocabulary under cross-entropy loss, while FAST ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) compresses action chunks via a discrete cosine transform and byte-pair encoding. Although these methods preserve the VLM architecture and training paradigm, control is moved from physical space into symbol space: token-level cross-entropy penalizes adjacent-bin and far-bin errors equally, and compressed tokens entangle multiple timesteps and dimensions so that a single token error can corrupt an entire trajectory. The second is computational and parameter decoupling . Continuous policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , GR00T N1 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , and X-VLA ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) preserve physical coordinates via flow matching or diffusion, but alter the model architecture and training paradigm by delegating trajectory generation to a dedicated action expert or 24-layer action Transformer outside the VLM. Because action supervision primarily updates the external expert and its competing gradients can degrade pretrained VLM features, Knowledge Insulation ( Driess et al., 2025 ) blocks expert gradients from entering the backbone—resolving training instability by hard-wiring architectural decoupling. Recent hybrids partially restore coupling along individual axes—sharing a backbone over discrete diffusion tokens ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , combining discrete and continuous branches ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , training a separate trajectory codec ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , or switching from discrete pretraining to downstream flow matching ( Ye et al., 2025 ) —yet none realizes a true eVLM that natively generates continuous physical trajectories while preserving its model architecture, its native pretraining paradigm, and its visual-language generalization.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: We instantiate this eVLM paradigm in Concertina through an end-to-end continuous latent action representation inside a diffusion VLM. Prior latent-action works (LAPA, IGOR, UniVLA, Moto, villa-X, CAT ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) ) show that mapping diverse robot controls into a shared latent space decouples embodiment-specific kinematics from sequence modeling, but they rely on separately pretrained VQ codebooks or trajectory codecs. We place this latent space directly inside the hidden space of a diffusion VLM (BARD-VL ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ): at each control timestep, a lightweight position-wise action encoder maps the complete D D -dimensional action vector into a single continuous latent action token in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , so a horizon- H H trajectory occupies H H tokens rather than H ​ D HD scalar symbols. Vision, language, and latent action tokens are jointly contextualized across every layer of the shared Transformer, and a lightweight position-wise action decoder maps output hidden states back to physical coordinates under direct coordinate reconstruction loss.

passages.text: Building on this principle, Concertina partitions the H H -step horizon into temporally ordered action blocks that are causal across blocks and bidirectional within each block, allowing contiguous action segments to be generated and refined jointly. During training, the multimodal conditioning prefix, corrupted action tokens, and teacher-forced clean action tokens are packed into a single sequence, supervising all block-conditional distributions in one forward pass and providing a compute-efficient, scalable end-to-end training path. Because the VLM backbone is already pretrained with masked block reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , Concertina reuses the exact same corrupt-and-reconstruct generative operator for continuous control without introducing a second training paradigm or external diffusion network.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: To rigorously test whether a policy acts as a decoupled VLA or a true eVLM—and to localize where action representation and trajectory computation reside—we introduce the Action Interface Audit , a checkpoint-level methodology comprising three metrics aligned with the three decoupling axes: (i) Error-Geometry Consistency ( EGC = p 95 / p 05 \mathrm{EGC}=p_{95}/p_{05} ), measuring whether unit training errors map stably to physical action errors; (ii) Trajectory Coupling Attribution (TCA) via the non-local response ratio ( NLR \mathrm{NLR} ), using deterministic finite differences to localize where cross-time dependencies emerge; and (iii) Action-Specific Capacity Ratio ( ASCR \mathrm{ASCR} ), quantifying parameters dedicated solely to action generation. The audit reveals that uniform discrete bins induce a 25.14 × 25.14\times physical-error span per single-token error and FAST-style compressed tokens suffer 77.9 % 77.9\% – 82.2 % 82.2\% structural decoding failures under single-token edits; π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} derive all cross-time coupling from external action experts ( ASCR = 16.51 % \mathrm{ASCR}=16.51\% and 19.17 % 19.17\% , rising to 22.19 % 22.19\% in SmolVLA and 35.10 % 35.10\% in X-VLA); whereas Concertina’s active action interfaces occupy only 0.21 % 0.21\% of the 4.46B model, exhibit zero cross-time response on their own ( NLR = 0 \mathrm{NLR}=0 ), and delegate all temporal trajectory coupling to the middle and late layers of the shared VLM backbone ( NLR = 4.06 % \mathrm{NLR}=4.06\% in pretraining, 4.10 % 4.10\% on CALVIN, and 1.22 % 1.22\% on LIBERO). Furthermore, a matched counterfactual intervention shows that attaching a second coordinate objective to the shared hidden space induces opposing gradients (cosine − 0.891 -0.891 ) and collapses CALVIN chain length from 2.970 2.970 to 0.237 0.237 , confirming that enabling native action generation in an eVLM without degrading the shared VLM requires co-designing the action representation and its supervision objective as a unified whole. On standard closed-loop benchmarks, Concertina reaches 98.15 % 98.15\% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9 % 85.9\% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC–D (Table 2 ).

passages.text: Our contributions are threefold:

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM) Paradigm. We formulate the eVLM paradigm, embodying manipulation and cognition within a single VLM across representation, supervision, and generation so that a pretrained VLM natively generates continuous action trajectories while preserving its model architecture, native training paradigm, and visual-language generalization.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: Continuous Blockwise eVLM Architecture (Concertina). We introduce Concertina, representing a horizon- H H trajectory as H H continuous latent action tokens with blockwise causal-bidirectional visibility and packed teacher forcing, requiring only 0.21 % 0.21\% active interface parameters and no external action expert, tokenizer, or codec.

passages.section: 1 Introduction
passages.location: 1 Introduction
passages.text: Action Interface Audit and Empirical Validation. We introduce EGC, TCA ( NLR \mathrm{NLR} ), and ASCR to audit representative discrete VLAs, action-expert VLAs, and our eVLM, provide counterfactual evidence on shared-space objective design, and demonstrate state-of-the-art closed-loop performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus alongside strong zero-shot transfer on CALVIN ABC–D.

passages.section: Latent action representations.
passages.location: Latent action representations.
passages.text: Several recent works learn compact latent action variables from video or robot demonstrations before policy learning. LAPA and IGOR extract discrete latent actions from action-free videos and image-goal pairs before grounding them into physical controls in a subsequent stage ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) , while UniVLA ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , Moto ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , villa-X ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and CAT ( Yang et al., 2026b ) introduce task-centric codebooks, motion tokens, proprioceptive latent dynamics, or frozen trajectory codecs. Because these methods freeze the tokenizer or codec prior to policy optimization, the latent space is never shaped directly by closed-loop physical control gradients. By contrast, Concertina embeds continuous actions directly into the hidden space of the diffusion VLM through lightweight position-wise projections co-trained end-to-end with the backbone under physical-coordinate reconstruction loss.

passages.section: External action experts versus shared-backbone generation.
passages.location: External action experts versus shared-backbone generation.
passages.text: Building on diffusion and flow-matching policies ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , continuous VLA architectures such as π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , GR00T N1 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , and X-VLA ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) preserve continuous control coordinates by pairing a VLM with a dedicated flow-matching action expert or a 24-layer external action Transformer, while OpenVLA-OFT attaches a continuous regression head ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Delegating trajectory generation to an external module separates motor computation from visual-language reasoning and introduces cross-module gradient tension; Knowledge Insulation ( Driess et al., 2025 ) addresses the resulting backbone degradation by blocking expert gradients from updating the VLM, permanently fixing the division between perception and control. Concertina eliminates the external action generator altogether, executing trajectory reconstruction inside the shared VLM Transformer so that manipulation and cognition co-adapt along a single parameter path.

passages.section: Discrete and compressed action tokenizers.
passages.location: Discrete and compressed action tokenizers.
passages.text: A third paradigm represents robot controls as discrete symbols over the language vocabulary. RT-2 and OpenVLA quantize each action coordinate into uniform bins ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) ; FAST compresses action chunks via a discrete cosine transform and byte-pair encoding ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) ; OAT learns ordered discrete action tokens ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ; and Discrete Diffusion VLA, MMaDA-VLA, and LLaDA-VLA apply masked discrete diffusion over quantized action tokens ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . Operating in symbol space decouples the training loss from physical error geometry: cross-entropy penalizes near-miss and large-displacement bin errors equally, while frequency-compressed tokens entangle multiple timesteps so that a single token error can invalidate an entire action chunk. Concertina retains token-level sequence length 𝒪 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{O}(H) while supervising every token directly in normalized physical coordinates.

passages.section: Blockwise diffusion VLMs.
passages.location: Blockwise diffusion VLMs.
passages.text: Blockwise diffusion models combine causal ordering across blocks with parallel bidirectional denoising within each block. BARD-VL bridges autoregressive and diffusion vision-language modeling via progressive block merging and stage-wise distillation over packed clean and corrupted sequences ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Recent VLA adaptations apply block diffusion to discretized action bins ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , combine autoregressive and continuous diffusion branches ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , or switch from discrete masked pretraining to downstream flow matching ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Concertina instead generalizes masked block reconstruction directly to continuous latent action vectors, turning the diffusion VLM itself into an eVLM that preserves both its shared backbone and its native pretraining operator (Figure 2 ).

passages.section: 3 Method
passages.location: 3 Method
passages.text: Concertina instantiates an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM) that embodies manipulation and cognition within a single diffusion vision-language model, enabling the pretrained backbone to natively generate continuous action trajectories without altering its model architecture or training paradigm. Its atomic generation unit is one complete continuous action vector at one control timestep, represented as a continuous latent action token: a lightweight position-wise encoder maps it into the VLM hidden space, and a position-wise decoder maps the contextualized hidden state back to physical control coordinates. All cross-time and cross-modal dependencies are modeled by the shared Transformer F θ F_{\theta} without an external action expert or discrete action tokenizer. This design establishes two direct coupling pathways between cognition and control: in the forward pass , action tokens attend to visual and linguistic representations at every Transformer layer rather than receiving a one-time conditioning summary; in the backward pass , physical-coordinate reconstruction gradients update the shared vision-language parameters end-to-end, consolidating manipulation experience into the backbone’s spatial representations.

passages.section: 4 Experiments
passages.location: 4 Experiments
passages.text: We evaluate Concertina across three questions: (i) how a single shared diffusion VLM performs on standard closed-loop manipulation benchmarks (Section 4.2 ); (ii) how blockwise partition topology, pretraining coordinate weighting, and shared-space objective design govern closed-loop control (Sections 4.3 – 4.4 ); and (iii) where trajectory representation, temporal coupling, and parameter capacity reside across VLA families under our Action Interface Audit (Section 4.5 ). Appendix B provides complete training recipes, inference configurations, and additional evaluations on decoding budgets, replanning frequency, and representation stress tests.

passages.section: 4.1 Evaluation protocol and scope
passages.location: 4.1 Evaluation protocol and scope
passages.text: Our main benchmark evaluation covers regular LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC–D ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Mees et al., 2021 ) . Regular LIBERO evaluates 50 episodes per task across four suites (LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-10; 2,000 episodes total); LIBERO-Plus evaluates all 10,030 perturbed tasks across the four suites; CALVIN ABC–D evaluates all 1,000 official five-task instruction chains in the unseen environment D after training on environments A, B, and C. We report success rate (%) on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and average completed chain length (AvgLen) alongside task- k k chain success rates (SR@ k k ) on CALVIN.

passages.section: Counterfactual dual-objective intervention.
passages.location: Counterfactual dual-objective intervention.
passages.text: Enabling a VLM to natively output continuous actions without degrading its pretrained representations requires care: when manipulation and cognition share a single hidden space, that space is not a passive feature buffer onto which incompatible coordinate readouts can be attached in parallel. We test this principle via a matched counterfactual intervention on the 8.35B shared-backbone checkpoint ( H = 25 H=25 ) that holds every model and optimization setting identical except for the supervision target: the single-objective baseline supervises relative actions alone, whereas the dual-objective variant attaches a frozen auxiliary decoder supervising absolute actions at loss weight 0.5 0.5 , with all 21/21 main action-interface tensors initialized bitwise identically from pretraining.

passages.section: Counterfactual dual-objective intervention.
passages.location: Counterfactual dual-objective intervention.
passages.text: Attaching the second coordinate target induces severe gradient conflict directly on the shared backbone hidden states (Figure 4 a–c). Across eight fixed CALVIN windows, the pooled cosine similarity between the relative main gradient and absolute auxiliary gradient on the shared hidden state is − 0.891 -0.891 , with 99 % 99\% of individual action-token gradients pointing in opposing directions. Even at weight 0.5 0.5 , the auxiliary gradient norm is 0.881 × 0.881\times the main gradient norm, reducing the cosine alignment between the combined gradient and the main objective to 0.474 0.474 . Inspecting the resulting parameter updates across all 26 trainable Transformer layers (Figure 4 b) reveals that while both runs make updates of virtually identical magnitude (relative L 2 L_{2} update norm rising from 4.6 % 4.6\% in shallow layers to 9.3 % 9.3\% in layers 17–22; overall norm ratio 1.003 × 1.003\times ), the parameter update direction cosine drops from 0.604 0.604 at Layer 2 down to 0.138 \mathbf{0.138} at Layer 22 (pooled cosine 0.225 0.225 )—precisely the middle and late layers where trajectory coupling resides. Consequently, teacher-forced main loss increases 5.12 × 5.12\times , one-pass position error increases 2.47 × 2.47\times , normalized MAE increases 1.60 × 1.60\times , and closed-loop CALVIN chain length drops by 92.0 % 92.0\% from 2.970 2.970 to 0.237 0.237 across 1,000 sequences (Figure 4 c). In a unified model, the action coordinate representation and its supervision objective jointly define the optimization geometry of the shared VLM backbone and must be co-designed as a single coherent interface.

passages.section: 5 Conclusion
passages.location: 5 Conclusion
passages.text: We presented Concertina, an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM) built on the principle that manipulation and cognition should be embodied within the same model rather than decoupled across a bolted-on VLA pipeline—enabling a pretrained diffusion VLM to natively output precise continuous actions while preserving its visual-language generalization, model architecture, and native training paradigm. By representing each control timestep as a continuous latent action token inside a shared diffusion VLM backbone and supervising temporally ordered action blocks directly in physical coordinates via packed teacher forcing, Concertina eliminates both discrete action tokenizers and external action experts while retaining the backbone’s native corrupt-and-reconstruct operator. Our Action Interface Audit across representative VLA families and Concertina demonstrates that an eVLM preserves unit error geometry ( EGC = 1 \mathrm{EGC}=1 ) and a full-rank 20D action manifold ( 18.63 / 20 18.63/20 effective rank), uses only 0.21 % 0.21\% active action-interface parameters ( ASCR \mathrm{ASCR} ), and forms cross-time trajectory coupling directly within the middle and late layers of the shared 36-layer VLM backbone ( NLR = 1.22 % \mathrm{NLR}=1.22\% – 4.10 % 4.10\% ). Controlled ablations further establish why blockwise bidirectional horizon partitioning ( K = 10 K=10 capturing 2.17 × 2.17\times more coherent action mass and yielding + 34.5 +34.5 points on LIBERO), physical coordinate weighting with state masking ( + 1.431 +1.431 and + 0.744 +0.744 CALVIN AvgLen), multi-block pretraining continuation ( + 0.208 +0.208 AvgLen over single-block continuation), and unified single-objective supervision with probability-valued gripper BCE ( + 0.427 +0.427 mean AvgLen across 8,000 factorial chains) are essential when manipulation and cognition share one hidden space. On standard closed-loop benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15 % 98.15\% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9 % 85.9\% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC–D.

passages.text: Concertina instantiates the shared diffusion VLM backbone F θ F_{\theta} from BARD-VL-B4-Mask-4B-Instruct ( Chen et al., 2026 ) (36 Transformer layers, hidden dimension d = 2560 d=2560 ) with a unified D = 20 D=20 canonical coordinate width supporting both single-arm and bimanual embodiments. Inactive embodiment dimensions are zeroed at the input and masked from the loss via the coordinate-validity indicator q n , d ∈ { 0 , 1 } q_{n,d}\in\{0,1\} (Figure 6 ).

passages.section: B.2 Multi-Embodiment Data Curation and Boundary Handling
passages.location: B.2 Multi-Embodiment Data Curation and Boundary Handling
passages.text: To ensure high trajectory quality across heterogeneous robot datasets, we apply an offline multi-stage curation pipeline prior to pretraining. The pipeline verifies timestamp continuity, finite coordinate ranges, and frame-to-action alignment across all 146,433 episodes. Non-informative static intervals are identified by cross-checking canonical end-effector velocity, joint motion channels, and visual optical flow, while semantic phase rules explicitly preserve functional holds such as gripper stabilization and pouring phases. Whenever a non-informative static segment is excised from a demonstration, the curation pipeline resets local episode boundaries so that each retained motion segment forms a contiguous trajectory, and windows crossing a segment boundary are padded using the explicit timestep-validity mask v n , i ∈ { 0 , 1 } v_{n,i}\in\{0,1\} .

passages.text: Because Concertina generates an entire K = 10 K=10 continuous action block within the shared VLM backbone, it supports both single-pass parallel decoding ( D = 1 , R = 0 D=1,R=0 : all 10 action tokens predicted in one backbone forward pass after prefix prefill) and multi-step risk-guided proposal and refinement ( D ≤ 4 , R = 0 D\leq 4,R=0 and D ≤ 4 , R = 5 D\leq 4,R=5 ). First, single-pass parallel generation ( D = 1 , R = 0 D=1,R=0 ) is already highly accurate: because the shared 36-layer VLM backbone jointly contextualizes all 10 action slots within the block, a single forward pass achieves 100.0 % 100.0\% (50/50) success on the LIBERO-Spatial benchmark subset in 102.40 102.40 mean steps and 3.92 3.92 AvgLen on CALVIN at 65.8 ​ ms 65.8\text{\,ms} per 10-step block ( 6.58 ​ ms 6.58\text{\,ms} per control step).
